title: XR-as-Stage: more-than-human worlding in extended reality for decentralized storytelling
abstract: XR-as-Stage is a framework for extended reality (XR) co-creation and techno-dramaturgy that builds shared worlds for decentralized storytelling. We describe how it opens imaginative play for more-than-human design, posthumous collaboration, and companion intelligences. XR-as-Stage operates in two coupled registers. The first is rehearsal, enabling lived relations to be explored through collaborative, low-stakes encounters, worlding futures together. The second is transformation, ephemeral actions becoming durable, iterable structures that can be revisited, altered, and built upon, designing futures together. Writeability couples the two: a rehearsal becomes a structure others can return to and rework, a way of rehearsing not just the future but reality together. We developed the approach through four of our own creative projects. The Middle is a webXR story commons, co-created asynchronously by rural communities navigating substance use disorder. Being In You stages presence with musician Cat Janice, across her life and death; her voice and creative legacy remain active through archives and ritual scenography. Fish Phone Booth places a single participant inside a dark booth to encounter marine life through spatial audio and bioacoustics. Live Action Robotic Role Play rehearses what care might look like when companion intelligences share the room. Together these projects show how XR can expand who and what gets to take part in worlding collective futures.

title: The digital transformation of grassroots agriculture: A text-mining analysis of Thai research portfolios
abstract: The concept of “Agriculture 4.0” promises to transform farming through the Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and big data, but in developing economies the technologies emphasized in policy may differ from those funded. This study evaluates the technological composition of Thailand’s public agricultural research portfolio as a retrospective baseline. The dataset contains 629 project records from four funding streams (Basic Research, NRCT, PMU-A and TSRI); the primary analysis covers the 579 projects funded in fiscal years 2020–2021, of which 406 with a specified technology descriptor were used for clustering and association tests, while 50 PMU-A projects from FY2024 were analyzed as a follow-up. We combined Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) features, latent semantic analysis, and K-Means clustering with Fisher’s exact and chi-square tests. Five exploratory innovation archetypes emerged: Agri-Processing & Product Engineering (n = 123), Digital Sensing & Resource Monitoring (n = 103), Green Production & Renewable Energy (n = 69), Value-Added Processing & Craft Textiles (n = 58), and Digital Platforms & Marketing (n = 53); cluster structure was weak (mean silhouette = 0.16), so the archetypes are interpreted cautiously. Funding agencies occupied distinct niches (χ²(12, N = 406) = 67.47, p < .001; Cramér’s V = 0.24). Three in four projects (76.2%) addressed a lack of skills, whereas water shortage (6.6%), soil issues (8.5%), and disaster risk (2.4%) were addressed far less often, mainly through GIS, sensing, and soil technologies. IoT projects were not disproportionately skills-oriented, indicating that the deployment gap is portfolio-wide rather than specific to IoT. These findings describe funded project descriptions, not field deployment. As a creative science contribution, the study offers a reproducible text-mining pipeline that funding agencies could apply in annual portfolio audits to compare funded research with strategic goals. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT HIGHLIGHTS Text mining of 579 Thai agricultural R&D projects (FY2020–2021) yields five exploratory innovation archetypes Three in four projects address a lack of skills; water, soil and disaster problems are each addressed by fewer than 9% Funding agencies occupy distinct technological niches (Cramér’s V = 0.24)

An Empirical Examination of Stakeholder Factors and Value-for-Money Audit Effectiveness in the Nigerian Public Service
journal: Sinergi International Journal of Management and Business
abstract: The systemic issues of poor stakeholder integration, low inclusiveness, and weak frameworks remain persistent and undermine the effectiveness of the VFM audit in Nigeria, raising serious concerns among scholars. This study examined how the application of stakeholder factors affects value-for-money (VFM) audit effectiveness within the Nigerian public service. This study used a quantitative cross-sectional design and a stratified random sample of 115 stakeholders (auditors, policymakers, civil servants, and representatives of civil society) from federal ministries, departments, and agencies (MDAs) in Nigeria, selected using the Yamane formula, with 106 responding. A structured questionnaire in Google Forms was used to obtain primary data. Analysis of quantitative data was done with SPSS v30 using descriptive statistics and regression analysis techniques. The results indicated that the effect of stakeholder influence (β = 0.356, p = 0.008) and auditors’ role (β = 0.421, p = 0.010) were significantly positive on VFM audit effectiveness. On the other hand, stakeholder engagement (β = -0.214, p = 0.132) inversely and insignificantly influenced the effectiveness of the VFM audit. The study established that stakeholder influence and auditors' roles are significant determinants of VFM audit effectiveness, while stakeholder engagement return is insignificant. The study recommends that the stakeholder engagement structures within the public service be redesigned in such a way that engagement is not cosmetic but more realistic and result-oriented.
